name: Entanglement Explained
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Spooky No More: How Entangled Qubits Correlate
lesson.summary: Defines entanglement as a joint state that cannot be factored into individual qubit descriptions, explains Bell states and correlated measurement outcomes, and corrects the faster-than-light misconception.
lesson.body:
A single qubit's state, as the previous sections described, is a superposition alpha|0⟩ + beta|1⟩. When you have two or more qubits, something new becomes possible that has no single qubit analogue: entanglement. A pair of qubits is entangled when their joint state cannot be written as a simple combination of one qubit's state and the other's separately. The standard example is the Bell state (1/√2)(|00⟩ + |11⟩). There is no way to pick individual states for qubit one and qubit two whose combination reproduces this. The two qubits have to be described together, as a single inseparable object, even if they are later carried far apart from each other.

What makes this physically strange is what happens upon measurement. If you measure the first qubit of that Bell state, you get 0 or 1 with equal probability, just as you would for an ordinary superposition. But the moment you learn that outcome, the second qubit's state is now fixed: if the first measurement gave 0, the second qubit will certainly also give 0 when measured, and if the first gave 1, the second will certainly give 1 too, no matter how far apart the two qubits are. Before either measurement, neither qubit had a definite value on its own. After one measurement, both outcomes are locked in together.

A limited, and explicitly imperfect, analogy is a pair of gloves shipped in two separate boxes to two different cities. If you open one box and find a left glove, you instantly know the other box holds a right glove, without needing to look. But that analogy describes ordinary classical correlation: the gloves had their handedness fixed all along, we just did not know it. Careful experiments, testing what are called Bell inequalities, have shown that entangled qubits are correlated more strongly than any such pre-arranged classical scheme could produce, across multiple choices of measurement setting. This line of experimental work, tracing back to tests of Bell's theorem, was recognized with the 2022 Nobel Prize in Physics, awarded to Alain Aspect, John Clauser, and Anton Zeilinger for their experiments establishing this result and helping found the field of quantum information science.

It is worth being direct about a common misconception here: entanglement does not allow faster than light communication. When you measure your half of an entangled pair, you get a random outcome that you cannot control, so you cannot use it to encode a chosen message. Only when the two experimenters later compare their results, through an ordinary classical channel that cannot exceed the speed of light, does the correlation become apparent. This is formalized in physics as the no communication theorem. The correlations are real and stronger than anything classical, but they do not let information travel instantaneously between the two locations.

Entanglement is not a curiosity, it is a working resource in quantum computing. Two qubit gates, such as the controlled NOT gate, take qubits that start in independent superpositions and entangle them, creating the kind of joint state described above. Later sections on the theoretical promise of quantum computing depend directly on this ability: it is the entangling operations between many qubits, combined with the interference discussed in the section on superposition, that let a quantum algorithm correlate computational paths in ways a classical computer's independent bits simply cannot replicate.
